Following instructions

This week’s behaviour focus

Following instructions

Pause. Listen. Check. Start.

20 minutes

Illustration created for this assembly

Discussion / choices: Pause. Listen. Check. Start. · Think · point · speak · watch

Key idea: Pause. Listen. Check. Start.

Presenter: Read every prompt and option aloud. Pupils may answer by pointing, thumbs, speaking, or simply watching. Staff operate the board; nobody needs to type. Allow processing time. Do not require eye contact or invite personal disclosures. Say: following instructions helps us learn, work together and stay safe. This is practice, not a test.

02 / 10 · Behaviour focus

What do instructions help us do?

1–2.5 min

Choose an idea. Explain why it matters.

A short instruction can help a whole group.

Discussion / choices: Stay safe · Work together · Get started

Key idea: All three matter. A useful instruction tells us what to do, and makes the next step clear.

Presenter: Take one or two ideas, then reveal all three. Link to an ordinary classroom task. Keep the focus on useful directions, not obedience without thought.

03 / 10 · Behaviour focus

The delivery desk

2.5–5 min

Watch. Pause. Predict the next move.

First: a vague direction. Then: a clear first step.

MADE BY MATT · ORIGINAL ANIMATIONOFFLINE

A delivery team hears: “Put it there.” The place and first step are unclear. Pause and ask: “Which item? Which place?” The instruction becomes: “Put the blue folder in tray A.” Hear the instruction. Check it. Start with one clear step.

PAUSE · PREDICT · REPLAY

Prediction point — what should happen next?

Captioned · no sound needed · pauses for your prediction

Scene summary / still alternative
  1. A delivery team hears: “Put it there.” The place and first step are unclear.
  2. Pause and ask: “Which item? Which place?”
  3. The instruction becomes: “Put the blue folder in tray A.”
  4. Hear the instruction. Check it. Start with one clear step.

Discussion / choices: What is missing from “put it there”? · What makes the next instruction useful?

Key idea: Clear words + a check + a first step help the team get the job done.

Presenter: Play the original animation. Pause at the prediction point; ask what information is missing. Replay if helpful. Ask: what changed in the clearer version? Do not interpret the scene as a test of intelligence or listening ability.

04 / 10 · Behaviour focus

Build the routine

5–7 min

Tap the steps in the order you would use them.

Start with a pause.

Discussion / choices: PAUSE: stop what you are doing when safe · LISTEN: hear the whole instruction · CHECK: be clear about the first step · START: make a start

Key idea: PAUSE → LISTEN → CHECK → START

Presenter: Correct order: PAUSE, LISTEN, CHECK, START. Explain: pause what you are doing when safe; hear the whole instruction; check the first step; make a start. Processing time is part of this routine.

05 / 10 · Behaviour focus

Spot the useful details

7–9 min

“Put the blue folder in tray A, then sit down.”

Tap the words that tell you what, where and the order.

Put the in , sit down.

WHAT: the blue folder

WHERE: tray A

ORDER: put the folder away first; then sit down

Discussion / choices: WHAT? blue folder · WHERE? tray A · ORDER? then sit down

Key idea: WHAT: blue folder. WHERE: tray A. ORDER: folder first, then sit down.

Presenter: Read the whole instruction once. Tap each useful detail. Ask how the message would change if we left that detail out. Explain that instructions should be short and manageable.

06 / 10 · Behaviour focus

Choose the next move

9–12 min

You are talking. Staff say: “Put the pen down and listen.”

Which response helps you catch the next instruction?

Discussion / choices: Keep talking · Argue about the pen · Pause and listen

Key idea: Pause and listen. You can ask a question when you have heard the instruction.

Presenter: Read all options without acting them out or imitating pupils. Each choice has an explanation. Use “Try another route” to compare. If a pupil raises a real concern, acknowledge it and offer a private conversation.

07 / 10 · Behaviour focus

When it is hard to start

12–14 min

Pick a barrier. Find a useful phrase.

Anyone can need an instruction explained another way.

Discussion / choices: “Can you say that again?” · “Which step first?” · “I need a moment, then help to start.” · “Can you show me?”

Key idea: Asking for help is part of following instructions.

Presenter: Use hypothetical examples; do not ask pupils to identify their own difficulty publicly. Adults should repeat or rephrase calmly, reduce the number of steps and allow processing time.

08 / 10 · Behaviour focus

Start, check or get help?

14–16 min

Read the request. Choose the useful response.

Choose a route for each situation.

Discussion / choices: Clear and safe → START · Unclear → CHECK · Unsafe → GET HELP

Key idea: Start a clear, safe task. Check an unclear instruction. Get help with something unsafe.

Presenter: Explain that pupils should not follow an unsafe request or keep a harmful secret. Choose trusted school staff for help. No pupil should be asked to share an experience. Correct sequence: START, CHECK, GET HELP.

09 / 10 · Behaviour focus

Practise one clear step

16–18 min

Listen to one instruction. Give it time.

“Point to the word START.”
You can point, look, say it or watch.

START

Discussion / choices: “Point to the word START.” · What helped make that instruction clear?

Key idea: A clear direction, time to process, and a check can help everyone begin.

Presenter: Read exactly: “Point to the word START.” Wait quietly, without counting down or requiring participation. Looking or watching is acceptable. Then ask: what helped? Model calm volume, one clear step and a pause.

10 / 10 · Behaviour focus

Your next useful step

18–20 min

Choose one thing you could try.

Keep it private if you prefer.

Discussion / choices: Pause to hear the instruction · Ask “Which step first?” · Start one clear step

Key idea: Pause. Listen. Check. Start. If it is unclear or unsafe, ask for help.

Presenter: No public pledge or repetition required. Accept any useful choice. End calmly and remind staff to give one manageable instruction at a time.

ASSEMBLY-FOLLOWING-INSTRUCTIONS

Word help

instruction
A direction that tells you what to do.
check
Make sure you understand the next step.
safe
Free from a danger you can reasonably avoid.
process
The steps used to reach a decision.

Take a moment

You can look away.
There is no answer needed right now.

Timers and animation are paused.

Teacher desk

20-minute assembly · secondary SEMH

Participation and delivery

Read every prompt and option aloud. Pupils may answer by pointing, thumbs, speaking, or simply watching. Staff operate the board; nobody needs to type. Allow processing time. Do not require eye contact or invite personal disclosures.

Use neutral examples. Do not turn the activities into a public behaviour test. If a real concern is raised, acknowledge it and arrange a private follow-up through school procedures.

The 20-minute route

MinutesStage

1–2.5What do instructions help us do?
2.5–5The delivery desk
5–7Build the routine
7–9Spot the useful details
9–12Choose the next move

14–16Start, check or get help?
16–18Practise one clear step
18–20Your next useful step

Timers never force a move and there is no alarm. If time slips, use fewer examples. Keep the final reminder.
